questions.question: Your agent stores memories for many users in one vector store. How should you keep Arjun's searches from returning Priya's memories?
options: Trust the embeddings; different users' memories will be dissimilar
Filter on a user metadata field before ranking
Use a higher k
Use a bigger embedding model
questions.explanation: Similarity says nothing about ownership. Filtering is a correctness feature.

questions.question: Why does the store normalise vectors to length 1 when they are written?
options: To save disk space
So cosine similarity becomes a plain dot product, with no division in the search loop
Because APIs return unnormalised vectors that are wrong
To make vectors shorter than 256 dimensions
questions.explanation: For unit vectors, dot(a, b) equals the cosine of the angle between them.

questions.question: What does upsert do when the text for an existing id has not changed?
options: Embeds it again to be safe
Updates the metadata and skips the embedding call, using a hash of the text to detect that nothing changed
Raises an error
Deletes the row
questions.explanation: Embedding calls cost money and time; a content hash avoids repeating them.

questions.question: Why does load() refuse a store built with a different embedding model?
options: The file format differs
Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so comparing them produces meaningless scores
To force upgrades
Because of licensing
questions.explanation: The scores would still look like similarities, which makes the bug very hard to notice.

questions.question: A query has no relevant memory, but top-3 search still returns three items. What prevents them from being put into the prompt as if they were relevant?
options: A larger k
A min_score threshold, set for this embedding model from a labelled test
Sorting by id
Chunking
questions.explanation: Thresholds differ between embedding models, so measure rather than guess.

questions.question: Your agent has 20,000 memories. Do you need an approximate (ANN) index?
options: Yes, always use HNSW
Probably not: an exact scan in NumPy or the database is usually fast enough at this size, and it never misses the true nearest neighbours
No, vector search doesn't work above 10,000 items
Yes, because exact search is inaccurate
questions.explanation: Brute force grows linearly; measure it before adding an index that trades recall for speed.
